claim: A transgenic mouse line containing GFP-tagged EB1 under the tetracycline-responsive element (TRE) promoter was generated.
source: To visualize and quantify microtubule dynamics in vivo, we generated a transgenic mouse containing a cassette encoding a GFP-tagged copy of the microtubule plus-tip tracking protein EB1 under the tetracycline-responsive element (TRE) promoter (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of the TRE-EB1-GFP mouse line with supporting figure.

claim: EB1-GFP expression in the TRE-EB1 mouse can be temporally controlled through doxycycline exposure.
source: With this line, EB1-GFP expression can be temporally controlled through doxycycline exposure and spatially controlled via cell- or tissue-specific tTA/rtTA lines (Urlinger et al., 2000) or tissue-specific Cre lines paired with the Rosa-rtTA line (Hochedlinger et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on tetracycline-responsive systems and describes the design of the system.

claim: EB1-GFP expression in the TRE-EB1 mouse can be spatially controlled via cell- or tissue-specific tTA/rtTA lines or tissue-specific Cre lines paired with the Rosa-rtTA line.
source: With this line, EB1-GFP expression can be temporally controlled through doxycycline exposure and spatially controlled via cell- or tissue-specific tTA/rtTA lines (Urlinger et al., 2000) or tissue-specific Cre lines paired with the Rosa-rtTA line (Hochedlinger et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on tetracycline-responsive systems and describes the design of the system.

claim: A TRE-EB1 mouse line with mosaic expression was chosen to allow precise resolution of single cells in a complex tissue field.
source: After screening founders by assaying EB1-GFP induction in primary keratinocytes, we chose a line with mosaic expression (hereafter referred to as TRE-EB1) to allow precise resolution of single cells in a complex tissue field.
evidence: The manuscript describes the screening process and rationale for selecting a specific founder line.

claim: EB1-GFP expression using the TRE-EB1 system does not cause cell morphology or tissue architecture phenotypes.
source: Importantly, we did not observe any cell morphology or tissue architecture phenotypes associated with EB1-GFP expression using this system.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from experiments using the TRE-EB1 system.

claim: Microtubules in basal keratinocytes grow from the cell center to the periphery in a roughly radial orientation.
source: Microtubules in basal keratinocytes grew from the cell center to the periphery in a roughly radial orientation, in agreement with previous data that the centrosome is the primary MTOC in these cells (Figure 1C, Video 1) (Lechler and Fuchs, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from live imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Video 1, and cites previous work.

claim: The centrosome is the primary MTOC in basal keratinocytes.
source: Microtubules in basal keratinocytes grew from the cell center to the periphery in a roughly radial orientation, in agreement with previous data that the centrosome is the primary MTOC in these cells (Figure 1C, Video 1) (Lechler and Fuchs, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work supporting this claim.

claim: In spinous cells, radial microtubule organization is lost and microtubules grow in all directions.
source: In spinous cells, clear radial organization was lost, and microtubules were observed growing in all directions (Figure 1C, Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from live imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Video 2.

claim: EB1 density is unaffected by the basal to spinous cell differentiation transition.
source: Despite the reorientation of microtubule growth in spinous cells, EB1 density was unaffected by this initial differentiation transition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Microtubules in granular cells grow throughout the cytoplasm in all directions.
source: Similar to spinous cells, microtubules in granular cells grow throughout the cytoplasm in all directions (Figure 1C, Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from live imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Video 3.

claim: The density of EB1-GFP puncta is higher in granular cells compared to basal and spinous cells.
source: However, the density of EB1-GFP puncta was higher in granular cells, and projections over time revealed that microtubules in these cells exhibited greatly reduced dynamics (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from imaging data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Microtubules in granular cells exhibit greatly reduced dynamics.
source: However, the density of EB1-GFP puncta was higher in granular cells, and projections over time revealed that microtubules in these cells exhibited greatly reduced dynamics (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from imaging data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Treatment of embryos with nocodazole eliminates EB1-GFP puncta.
source: Treatment of embryos with nocodazole eliminated the GFP puncta, strongly suggesting that these EB1-GFP comets mark plus-ends of very slowly growing and/or paused microtubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EB1-GFP comets mark plus-ends of very slowly growing and/or paused microtubules in granular cells.
source: Treatment of embryos with nocodazole eliminated the GFP puncta, strongly suggesting that these EB1-GFP comets mark plus-ends of very slowly growing and/or paused microtubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the nocodazole treatment experiment.

claim: Microtubule growth distance gradually decreases over keratinocyte differentiation.
source: Quantification of microtubule growth distances revealed a gradual decrease in motility over keratinocyte differentiation (Figure 1E, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: The gradual decrease in microtubule growth distance during keratinocyte differentiation is due to two changes in microtubule behavior that occur at distinct differentiation transitions.
source: Surprisingly, this gradual decrease in microtubule growth distance was due to two changes in microtubule behavior that occurred at distinct differentiation transitions.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the quantification data to identify two distinct changes.

claim: Microtubule growth speed is relatively unaffected at the basal to spinous cell transition.
source: At the basal to spinous cell transition, microtubule growth speed was relatively unaffected, although there was a minor increase in growth speed in spinous cells (basal mean growth speed 11.1 ± 3.1 µm/min versus spinous mean growth speed 12.2 ± 3.3 µm/min) (Figure 1F, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 1F and Table 1.

claim: There is a minor increase in microtubule growth speed in spinous cells compared to basal cells (basal mean growth speed 11.1 ± 3.1 µm/min versus spinous mean growth speed 12.2 ± 3.3 µm/min).
source: At the basal to spinous cell transition, microtubule growth speed was relatively unaffected, although there was a minor increase in growth speed in spinous cells (basal mean growth speed 11.1 ± 3.1 µm/min versus spinous mean growth speed 12.2 ± 3.3 µm/min) (Figure 1F, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 1F and Table 1.

claim: Microtubule growth rates observed in vivo in keratinocytes are similar to those observed in vivo in cells of the C. elegans egg-laying apparatus and in mouse muscle.
source: These growth rates were similar to those observed in vivo in cells of the C. elegans egg-laying apparatus and in mouse muscle (Lacroix et al., 2014; Oddoux et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript compares the observed growth rates to previously published data.

claim: Microtubule growth speeds are strongly suppressed as spinous cells differentiate into granular cells (granular mean growth speed 7.1 ± 3.7 µm/min).
source: In contrast, microtubule growth speeds were strongly suppressed as spinous cells differentiated into granular cells (granular mean growth speed 7.1 ± 3.7 µm/min) (Figure 1F, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 1F and Table 1.

claim: Microtubule growth duration is significantly shorter in spinous versus basal keratinocytes.
source: Examination of the persistence of a single EB1-GFP puncta revealed that growth duration was significantly shorter in spinous versus basal keratinocytes (Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Microtubule growth duration is unchanged between spinous and granular cells.
source: The growth duration was unchanged between spinous and granular cells.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification results.

claim: The short microtubule growth periods likely reflect pause and/or catastrophe events that cannot be discriminated because EB1-GFP marks only growing microtubules.
source: The short growth periods likely reflect pause and/or catastrophe events that cannot be discriminated because EB1-GFP marks only growing microtubules.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the observed short growth periods based on the properties of EB1-GFP.

claim: There is no correlation between microtubule growth speed and duration in basal, spinous, and granular cells (R2 = 0.002–0.19).
source: While there was no correlation between the growth speed and duration (R2 = 0.002–0.19) or the growth speed and distance (R2 = 0.004–0.2), there was a clear correlation between the length of time an EB1-GFP puncta moved and how far it traveled in basal (R2 = 0.87) and spinous cells (R2 = 0.85), as would be expected for microtubules polymerizing at a constant speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is no correlation between microtubule growth speed and distance in basal, spinous, and granular cells (R2 = 0.004–0.2).
source: While there was no correlation between the growth speed and duration (R2 = 0.002–0.19) or the growth speed and distance (R2 = 0.004–0.2), there was a clear correlation between the length of time an EB1-GFP puncta moved and how far it traveled in basal (R2 = 0.87) and spinous cells (R2 = 0.85), as would be expected for microtubules polymerizing at a constant speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a clear correlation between the length of time an EB1-GFP puncta moved and how far it traveled in basal cells (R2 = 0.87).
source: While there was no correlation between the growth speed and duration (R2 = 0.002–0.19) or the growth speed and distance (R2 = 0.004–0.2), there was a clear correlation between the length of time an EB1-GFP puncta moved and how far it traveled in basal (R2 = 0.87) and spinous cells (R2 = 0.85), as would be expected for microtubules polymerizing at a constant speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a clear correlation between the length of time an EB1-GFP puncta moved and how far it traveled in spinous cells (R2 = 0.85).
source: While there was no correlation between the growth speed and duration (R2 = 0.002–0.19) or the growth speed and distance (R2 = 0.004–0.2), there was a clear correlation between the length of time an EB1-GFP puncta moved and how far it traveled in basal (R2 = 0.87) and spinous cells (R2 = 0.85), as would be expected for microtubules polymerizing at a constant speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correlation between microtubule growth time and distance is greatly reduced in granular cells (R2 = 0.23).
source: Interestingly, this correlation is greatly reduced in granular cells (R2 = 0.23), (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Absolute microtubule polymerization rates are dramatically increased in isolated primary keratinocytes compared to in vivo.
source: Absolute polymerization rates were dramatically increased in isolated cells, suggesting that microtubule dynamics are altered as primary cells initiate a wound-healing response in culture, as has been noted for cell-cell junctions (Figure 1D–G) (Foote et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 1D-G and cites previous work on cell-cell junctions.

claim: Microtubule dynamics are altered as primary keratinocytes initiate a wound-healing response in culture.
source: Absolute polymerization rates were dramatically increased in isolated cells, suggesting that microtubule dynamics are altered as primary cells initiate a wound-healing response in culture, as has been noted for cell-cell junctions (Figure 1D–G) (Foote et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observed differences and cites previous work.

claim: The overall trends in microtubule dynamics across all three measured parameters in cultured primary keratinocytes mirror the trends seen at the basal to spinous transition in vivo.
source: Interestingly, although the absolute polymerization rate was greatly increased, the overall trends across all three measured parameters consistently mirrored the trends seen at the basal to spinous transition in vivo (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: The manuscript compares quantification data from cultured cells to in vivo data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Cultured primary keratinocytes do not fully recapitulate the physiological setting for microtubule dynamics.
source: These data highlight that while there is some utility in assessing microtubule dynamics in cultured cells, they do not fully recapitulate the physiological setting.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the comparison between in vivo and in vitro data.

claim: Microtubules reorganize into non-centrosomal arrays as basal keratinocytes differentiate.
source: We used this line to make qualitative observations about microtubule organization during differentiation that confirmed that microtubules reorganize into non-centrosomal arrays as basal cells differentiate.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from the TRE-EB1 mouse line.

claim: Pause/catastrophe events are initially increased as basal cells differentiate into spinous cells.
source: Interestingly, by following microtubule dynamics over distinct differentiation transitions, we demonstrate that pause/catastrophe events are initially increased as basal cells differentiate into spinous cells.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the quantification data on microtubule dynamics.

claim: As spinous cells mature into granular cells, microtubule polymerization rates are strongly suppressed.
source: As spinous cells mature into granular cells, microtubule polymerization rates are strongly suppressed and the occurrence of very slow growing microtubules increases significantly.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the quantification data on microtubule dynamics.

claim: As spinous cells mature into granular cells, the occurrence of very slow growing microtubules increases significantly.
source: As spinous cells mature into granular cells, microtubule polymerization rates are strongly suppressed and the occurrence of very slow growing microtubules increases significantly.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the quantification data on microtubule dynamics.

claim: A transgenic mouse line containing HA-tagged spastin M85 under the TRE promoter was generated.
source: Therefore, we placed the highly active M85 spastin isoform with an N-terminal HA tag under the TRE promoter, hereafter referred to as TRE-spastin (Figure 2A) (Solowska et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of the TRE-spastin mouse line with supporting figure and citation.

claim: Spastin overexpression is sufficient to dramatically perturb microtubule organization in numerous cell types.
source: Spastin is a single-subunit microtubule severing protein whose overexpression is sufficient to dramatically perturb microtubule organization in numerous cell types (Le Droguen et al., 2015; Quintin et al., 2016; Sherwood et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work demonstrating spastin's effects.

claim: Spastin expression in transfected keratinocytes is only detected upon doxycycline administration.
source: Spastin expression was only detected upon doxycycline administration, demonstrating that TRE-spastin can be temporally controlled in cultured cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes validation experiments in cultured cells.

claim: All keratinocytes containing detectable spastin expression show almost complete loss of microtubules.
source: Importantly, all cells containing detectable spastin expression showed almost complete loss of microtubules, indicating that even low levels of spastin OE are sufficient to severely compromise microtubule organization (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from cultured cell experiments shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Even low levels of spastin overexpression are sufficient to severely compromise microtubule organization.
source: Importantly, all cells containing detectable spastin expression showed almost complete loss of microtubules, indicating that even low levels of spastin OE are sufficient to severely compromise microtubule organization (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that all spastin-expressing cells show microtubule loss.

claim: Robust spastin overexpression is detected in CMV-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice within 24 hr of doxycycline administration.
source: We detected robust spastin OE in CMV-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice within 24 hr of doxycycline administration, and we did not detect HA expression in doxycycline-treated TRE-spastin mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No HA expression is detected in doxycycline-treated TRE-spastin mice without rtTA.
source: We detected robust spastin OE in CMV-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice within 24 hr of doxycycline administration, and we did not detect HA expression in doxycycline-treated TRE-spastin mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CMV-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice rapidly lose weight following doxycycline administration.
source: CMV-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice rapidly lost weight and had macroscopic alterations to some organs (Figure 2F and data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CMV-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice have macroscopic alterations to some organs following doxycycline administration.
source: CMV-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice rapidly lost weight and had macroscopic alterations to some organs (Figure 2F and data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations.

claim: Spastin overexpression greatly reduces α-tubulin signal in all tissues assayed.
source: Importantly, spastin OE greatly reduced α-tubulin signal in all tissues assayed; often only small fragments of MTs remained following spastin induction (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 2G and 2H.

claim: Only small fragments of microtubules often remain following spastin induction in tissues.
source: Importantly, spastin OE greatly reduced α-tubulin signal in all tissues assayed; often only small fragments of MTs remained following spastin induction (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 2G and 2H.

claim: Spastin overexpression dramatically shortens cilia.
source: In addition to cytoplasmic microtubules, spastin OE also dramatically shortened cilia, although it is unclear if this treatment shortens existing cilia or perturbs new cilia growth (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 2G.

claim: It is unclear if spastin overexpression shortens existing cilia or perturbs new cilia growth.
source: In addition to cytoplasmic microtubules, spastin OE also dramatically shortened cilia, although it is unclear if this treatment shortens existing cilia or perturbs new cilia growth (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism of cilia shortening.

claim: Between 20–40% of basal cells overexpress spastin in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice.
source: Between 20–40% of basal cells overexpressed spastin using this strategy (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spastin overexpression perturbs microtubule organization in basal keratinocytes.
source: Spastin OE perturbed microtubule organization in basal cells and, as expected, induced a dramatic increase in mitotically arrested cells in mutant tissue (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Spastin overexpression induces a dramatic increase in mitotically arrested cells in basal keratinocytes.
source: Spastin OE perturbed microtubule organization in basal cells and, as expected, induced a dramatic increase in mitotically arrested cells in mutant tissue (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Only spastin-positive cells in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin tissue have uniformly unaligned, condensed chromosomes.
source: Only spastin-positive cells in mutant tissue had uniformly unaligned, condensed chromosomes, demonstrating that spastin OE in basal keratinocytes caused a mitotic arrest in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Spastin overexpression in basal keratinocytes causes mitotic arrest in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Only spastin-positive cells in mutant tissue had uniformly unaligned, condensed chromosomes, demonstrating that spastin OE in basal keratinocytes caused a mitotic arrest in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript infers cell-autonomous mitotic arrest from the observation that only spastin-positive cells show the phenotype.

claim: Increased apoptosis is observed in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis, presumably due to mitotic catastrophe.
source: Consequently, we observed increased apoptosis, presumably due to mitotic catastrophe, and a tissue-wide hyper-proliferative response to maintain progenitor number (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3G and 3H and infers the cause.

claim: A tissue-wide hyper-proliferative response occurs in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis to maintain progenitor number.
source: Consequently, we observed increased apoptosis, presumably due to mitotic catastrophe, and a tissue-wide hyper-proliferative response to maintain progenitor number (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3G and 3H and infers the purpose.

claim: K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis remains architecturally normal with no detectable barrier defects at the level of spastin induction achieved.
source: At this level of induction, the tissue remained architecturally normal with no detectable barrier defects, demonstrating that the epidermis is highly robust to perturbations in basal keratinocytes (Figure 3I).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The epidermis is highly robust to perturbations in basal keratinocytes.
source: At this level of induction, the tissue remained architecturally normal with no detectable barrier defects, demonstrating that the epidermis is highly robust to perturbations in basal keratinocytes (Figure 3I).
evidence: The manuscript infers robustness from the observation that tissue architecture and barrier function are maintained despite perturbations.

claim: Spastin-positive cells are observed in the upper layers of the epidermis after several days of induction in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice.
source: Interestingly, we noted spastin-positive cells in the upper layers of the epidermis after several days of induction in the K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin line.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations.

claim: Suprabasal spastin-positive cells in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis express keratin 5/14.
source: These suprabasal spastin-positive cells expressed keratin 5/14, which are normally exclusively expressed in basal keratinocytes (Figure 3J).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Keratin 5/14 are normally exclusively expressed in basal keratinocytes.
source: These suprabasal spastin-positive cells expressed keratin 5/14, which are normally exclusively expressed in basal keratinocytes (Figure 3J).
evidence: The manuscript states established knowledge about keratin 5/14 expression.

claim: No mis-expression of the K14-rtTA transgene is detected in suprabasal layers.
source: As we have not detected any mis-expression of the K14-rtTA transgene, this result suggests that spastin-expressing cells delaminated from the basement membrane.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from validation experiments.

claim: Spastin-expressing cells delaminate from the basement membrane in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis.
source: As we have not detected any mis-expression of the K14-rtTA transgene, this result suggests that spastin-expressing cells delaminated from the basement membrane.
evidence: The manuscript infers delamination from the presence of suprabasal spastin-positive cells expressing basal markers without rtTA mis-expression.

claim: Many mitotically arrested cells appear to be in the process of delaminating in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis.
source: Indeed, we identified many mitotically arrested cells that appeared to be in the process of delaminating, suggesting that spastin-positive cells in the suprabasal layers were generated, at least partially, through delamination (Figure 3K).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Spastin-positive cells in the suprabasal layers of K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis are generated, at least partially, through delamination.
source: Indeed, we identified many mitotically arrested cells that appeared to be in the process of delaminating, suggesting that spastin-positive cells in the suprabasal layers were generated, at least partially, through delamination (Figure 3K).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from observations of delaminating mitotically arrested cells.

claim: The epidermis eliminates mitotically arrested cells from the proliferative niche through apoptosis or delamination.
source: Thus, the epidermis eliminates mitotically arrested cells from the proliferative niche either through apoptosis or delamination.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from observations of increased apoptosis and delamination.

claim: Areas with numerous suprabasal spastin-positive cells display local thickening in K14-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis.
source: Areas with numerous suprabasal spastin-positive cells displayed local thickening, suggesting that disruption of microtubules in suprabasal keratinocytes may more severely disrupt epidermal architecture (Figure 3J).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Disruption of microtubules in suprabasal keratinocytes may more severely disrupt epidermal architecture than disruption in basal cells.
source: Areas with numerous suprabasal spastin-positive cells displayed local thickening, suggesting that disruption of microtubules in suprabasal keratinocytes may more severely disrupt epidermal architecture (Figure 3J).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation of local thickening in areas with suprabasal spastin-positive cells.

claim: A BAC transgenic mouse line was generated in which rtTA is expressed from a large region of the keratin 10 promoter.
source: Therefore, we generated a BAC transgenic in which rtTA is expressed from a large region of the keratin 10 promoter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of the K10-rtTA mouse line with supporting figure.

claim: K10-rtTA faithfully recapitulates endogenous K10 expression in both embryos and adults.
source: Using TRE-H2B-GFP mice, we validated that K10-rtTA faithfully recapitulates endogenous K10 expression in both embryos and adults (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes validation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: K10-rtTA induction is observed in e14.5 epidermis as stratification commences.
source: K10-rtTA induction was observed in e14.5 epidermis, as stratification commences, and was robustly and uniformly induced by e15.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) (Tumbar et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and cites previous work on stratification timing.

claim: K10-rtTA induction is robustly and uniformly induced by e15.5.
source: K10-rtTA induction was observed in e14.5 epidermis, as stratification commences, and was robustly and uniformly induced by e15.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) (Tumbar et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Robust K10-rtTA expression is observed in all K10-expressing tissues assayed, with the exception of the embryonic dorsal tongue.
source: Robust expression was observed in all K10-expressing tissues assayed, with the exception of the embryonic dorsal tongue, which only exhibited minimal induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: The embryonic dorsal tongue exhibits only minimal K10-rtTA induction.
source: Robust expression was observed in all K10-expressing tissues assayed, with the exception of the embryonic dorsal tongue, which only exhibited minimal induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: H2B-GFP expression is only detected in cells that endogenously express K10 in K10-rtTA mice.
source: Importantly, H2B-GFP expression was only detected in cells that endogenously express K10, demonstrating that our K10-rtTA line is a powerful tool to reliably control expression exclusively in post-mitotic suprabasal cells, thereby bypassing any potential mitotic abnormalities that may result from perturbations utilizing the widely adopted K14-rtTA and K5/14-Cre systems.
evidence: The manuscript describes validation experiments.

claim: The K10-rtTA line is a powerful tool to reliably control expression exclusively in post-mitotic suprabasal cells.
source: Importantly, H2B-GFP expression was only detected in cells that endogenously express K10, demonstrating that our K10-rtTA line is a powerful tool to reliably control expression exclusively in post-mitotic suprabasal cells, thereby bypassing any potential mitotic abnormalities that may result from perturbations utilizing the widely adopted K14-rtTA and K5/14-Cre systems.
evidence: The manuscript infers the utility of the K10-rtTA line from validation experiments.

claim: The K10-rtTA line bypasses potential mitotic abnormalities that may result from perturbations utilizing K14-rtTA and K5/14-Cre systems.
source: Importantly, H2B-GFP expression was only detected in cells that endogenously express K10, demonstrating that our K10-rtTA line is a powerful tool to reliably control expression exclusively in post-mitotic suprabasal cells, thereby bypassing any potential mitotic abnormalities that may result from perturbations utilizing the widely adopted K14-rtTA and K5/14-Cre systems.
evidence: The manuscript infers this advantage from the specificity of K10-rtTA expression in post-mitotic cells.

claim: Spastin is expressed on average in 77% of suprabasal cells in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice.
source: We confirmed that spastin expression was confined to post-mitotic suprabasal keratinocytes by HA staining and found that spastin was expressed on average in 77% of suprabasal cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Spastin expression is confined to post-mitotic suprabasal keratinocytes in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice.
source: We confirmed that spastin expression was confined to post-mitotic suprabasal keratinocytes by HA staining and found that spastin was expressed on average in 77% of suprabasal cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin neonates are recognizable from control littermates.
source: Mutant neonates were recognizable from control littermates, and some exhibited flaky skin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Some K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin neonates exhibit flaky skin.
source: Mutant neonates were recognizable from control littermates, and some exhibited flaky skin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Spastin overexpression in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice leads to severe thickening of the epidermis.
source: Surprisingly, spastin OE in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice led to a severe thickening of the epidermis and disruptions to epidermal architecture (Figure 4C–E), phenotypes not predicted by prior studies.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Spastin overexpression in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice leads to disruptions to epidermal architecture.
source: Surprisingly, spastin OE in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice led to a severe thickening of the epidermis and disruptions to epidermal architecture (Figure 4C–E), phenotypes not predicted by prior studies.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: The epidermal thickening and architecture disruptions in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice are phenotypes not predicted by prior studies.
source: Surprisingly, spastin OE in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin mice led to a severe thickening of the epidermis and disruptions to epidermal architecture (Figure 4C–E), phenotypes not predicted by prior studies.
evidence: The manuscript notes that these phenotypes were unexpected based on prior literature.

claim: The increased thickness of K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis is associated with an increase in the number of cell layers.
source: We found that the increased thickness of the mutant epidermis was associated with an increase in the number of cell layers (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The increase in cell number in K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis is due to specific hyperproliferation of basal progenitor cells.
source: This increase in cell number was due to a specific hyperproliferation of basal progenitor cells, as no proliferation was noted in the suprabasal cell compartment (Figure 4F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: No proliferation is noted in the suprabasal cell compartment of K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin epidermis.

evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observed severe phenotypes.

claim: The epidermis eliminates basal cells by delamination/differentiation, allowing the epidermis to make use of these defective progenitors.
source: The elimination of basal cells by delamination/differentiation allows the epidermis to make use of these defective progenitors.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the observed delamination phenotype.

claim: Stable non-centrosomal microtubules regulate overall tissue architecture in the epidermis.
source: By overexpressing spastin in suprabasal keratinocytes using a novel K10-rtTA mouse, we demonstrate that stable non-centrosomal microtubules regulate overall tissue architecture.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from the K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin experiments.

claim: Defects in cell shape appear to be one clear cell-autonomous consequence of microtubule disruption in differentiated keratinocytes.
source: While there are pleiotropic phenotypes downstream of microtubule loss in differentiated keratinocytes, defects in cell shape appear to be one clear cell-autonomous consequence of microtubule disruption.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from the K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin experiments.

claim: Differentiation-induced flattening occurs in the absence of E-cadherin, type II myosins and the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Differentiation-induced flattening occurs in the absence of E-cadherin, type II myosins and the Arp2/3 complex, which clearly impact cell shape in numerous other cell types (Sumigray et al., 2012; Tinkle et al., 2004; Tunggal et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on these proteins.

claim: E-cadherin, type II myosins and the Arp2/3 complex clearly impact cell shape in numerous other cell types.
source: Differentiation-induced flattening occurs in the absence of E-cadherin, type II myosins and the Arp2/3 complex, which clearly impact cell shape in numerous other cell types (Sumigray et al., 2012; Tinkle et al., 2004; Tunggal et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on these proteins.

claim: Kinesin-dependent microtubule sliding may provide a force to drive cell-shape changes in keratinocytes.
source: An intriguing possibility is that kinesin-dependent microtubule sliding may provide a force to drive cell-shape changes, similar to what has been reported in neurons (Winding et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a speculative mechanism and cites previous work in neurons.

claim: While microtubules are required for initiating flattening in keratinocytes, they are dispensable for maintaining the flattened granular shape, which could be controlled by other cytoskeletal elements like keratins.
source: Interestingly, our data also indicate that, while microtubules are required for initiating flattening, they are dispensable for maintaining the flattened granular shape, which could be controlled by other cytoskeletal elements like keratins.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the short-term spastin induction and nocodazole treatment experiments.

claim: One of the clear strengths of the TRE-spastin mouse is the ability to distinguish between cell-autonomous and tissue-wide effects of microtubule disruption.
source: One of the clear strengths of the TRE-spastin mouse is the ability to distinguish between cell-autonomous and tissue-wide effects of microtubule disruption.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the utility of the TRE-spastin mouse.

claim: Spastin overexpression in suprabasal keratinocytes uncovered numerous unexpected non-cell-autonomous defects including desmosome perturbation, basal hyperproliferation, cornified envelope defects, and premature differentiation.
source: Spastin OE in suprabasal keratinocytes uncovered numerous unexpected non-cell-autonomous defects associated with loss of microtubules in differentiated cells. These included desmosome perturbation, basal hyperproliferation, cornified envelope defects, and premature differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from the K10-rtTA; TRE-spastin experiments.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the non-cell-autonomous effects of microtubule disruption in differentiated keratinocytes are a clear area for future study.
source: The mechanisms underlying these effects are a clear area for future study.
evidence: The manuscript proposes future research directions.

claim: It remains important to identify how cells sense microtubule loss.
source: Particularly, it remains important to identify how cells sense microtubule loss, whether the signal is mechanical in nature or more directly involves sensing tubulin/microtubule levels or organization.
evidence: The manuscript proposes future research questions.

claim: The signal by which cells sense microtubule loss may be mechanical in nature or may more directly involve sensing tubulin/microtubule levels or organization.
source: Particularly, it remains important to identify how cells sense microtubule loss, whether the signal is mechanical in nature or more directly involves sensing tubulin/microtubule levels or organization.
evidence: The manuscript proposes alternative speculative mechanisms.

claim: The work presented highlights the value of examining phenotypes associated with microtubule disruption in vivo.
source: The work presented here highlights the value of examining phenotypes associated with microtubule disruption in vivo, and these tools should be of broad utility to the study of microtubules during mammalian development and homeostasis.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the significance of the work.

claim: The TRE-EB1 and TRE-spastin tools should be of broad utility to the study of microtubules during mammalian development and homeostasis.
source: The work presented here highlights the value of examining phenotypes associated with microtubule disruption in vivo, and these tools should be of broad utility to the study of microtubules during mammalian development and homeostasis.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the utility of the tools developed.
